posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: The original r/legoleak post mentioned Lego took the announcement down as it might have been revealed prematurely. If so, I can imagine the official announcement potentially mentioning two mash-up sets being due next year (and might even impose specific limitations to ensure people don’t cover specific subject matter). I agree it’s an exciting competition though, there’s a lot of potential in it even with the Star Wars aspect being limited to ANH. My disappointment over the lack of August playsets aside, I wonder what the second mashup set is going to be beyond the likely aspect of it being an enemy vehicle for the Iron Falcon to fight against. Love these, I had a Rex and Winter Soldier mashup in mind too. Called it! Plus we already have a Yoda, Rex, and Pilot Luke maxifig covering the buildable character side of things next year. Although I’m suspicious there are no droid characters in that lineup yet. My high-level guesses are: - $70: G-17 Imperial Reaper, going by the trailer it seems like a 1-2 person fighter anyway, - $90: Some cool-looking enemy vehicle belonging to Matt Smith and Mia Goth’s faction, - $170: The big starship vehicle we see in the trailer escaping the helmeted troopers. I rewatched the D23 Starfighter trailer and even though it’s not much to go on (yet), I did like what I saw and have a lot of high hopes for the film. Hopefully some marketing will begin kicking off around December.

posts.title: A Practical Lego Mechanical Skeleton Clock | Deco Clock II
posts.text: Introducing Deco Clock II, a Lego mechanical skeleton clock that can fit easily into any stand or shelf. Long story short, a previous wall clock I published on YouTube did not perform well in the long term because of inherent flaws in the structure and using parts that were used instead of new. Hanging a clock structure off a wall with a heavy pendulum and weight demands a great amount of structural engineering, and I wanted something that had less uncertainty with how sturdy the structure was. This saga has ostensibly turned into a second version of this clock, one which is designed with long-term performance, practicality, and similar aesthetics in mind. I want people to easily be able to get into the hobby, and this clock is designed with long-term performance and ease-of-set up in mind. In my opinion, most mechanical Lego clocks fail at many of the listed aspects below (aside from some of David’s and KEvron’s pieces, and even those require custom stands or shelves). Yes, this stand is one you need to supply yourself. Although, it can either be easily bought or assembled in whatever kit it comes with online, does not need any modifications to your walls, does not need any custom tools or jobs, can easily be moved around, and can even display other things on the lower shelves within the stand. A clock with that in mind needs the following things, which this one satisfies: Actually tells accurate time. Has instructions Has good, reliable mechanisms (The class-leading David Ziemkiewicz’s 64t grasshopper escapement). Easily modifiable Runs for a full day 100% original Lego Looks like it can be a real decoration. No electronics The structure it sits on does not require any tools or custom jobs. The entire thing can easily be moved to different areas. The structure is sound and made with sturdy Technic bricks rather than feeble Technic lift arms. The large PDF guide will be on Rebrickable soon and has everything you need to know to set it up. Guide for now here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/19oCEW1kYmrOvCebuSBKqhcnur89A68zu/view?usp=drive_link I’m happy to answer any questions at: therealfabulousfox@gmail.com. See the full, detailed video on my YouTube channel.

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: @Davidz90 Thanks a lot for sharing all these construction details and photos with me! It’s really interesting to see that, even though we took different paths, many of the solutions you explored are identical to the ones I tested and, in some cases, adopted myself (such as offsetting the two rings by 45° and using rollers at the base). I also tried using the outer grooves to constrain and guide the rings, supporting their weight with bearings made from rubberized wheels. For the groove guides, I used the **1x1 Round Tiles with Bar / Pin (Part #20482)**. In the end, I moved away from that approach and allowed the rings to rest naturally by gravity on the support wheels, held in place by the drive pinion. In early versions, I used two 8t pinions (for a higher reduction ratio and less required torque), but after encountering a few issues with mesh and stability, I switched to a single 12t drive pinion. I'll definitely experiment with the magnetic hand concept for fun, though as you noted, it won't be something I can submit on the LEGO Ideas portal. Thanks again for sharing your work!

posts.title: Cylinder advice
posts.text: cylinders + pilot truck + R40 curves = impossible to get everything cylinders + pilot truck + R104 curves = still very difficult to get everything I find that I need to balance the motion of the pilot truck with where the cylinders go and how large to make them. Often the backsides of my cylinders are empty spaces so the pilot wheels can slip in the space on a curve and I try to put the front of the cylinders between the wheels on the pilot truck. That way, I can do a one wide support in the truck to minimize conflict with the front of the cylinder. So effectively the "cylinders" become an L-shaped shell that look good from the front and side. Other times I build to be operational on R40 switches because R40 yards are so much more space efficient. So then I have to get really creative, e.g., for my streamlined SP Pacific

posts.title: Tatra 813 AM-50 (Bridge layer)
posts.text: Hi everyone! I’ve been planning to build this model for years, but the time was finally right, and my Tatra 813 chassis is now sufficiently refined to carry heavier superstructures while maintaining high off-road capability. I had the model roughly assembled in five days, with another three days spent on fine-tuning. The chassis is powered by two Buwizz RC motors; steering is handled by a PF servo motor, and a CaDA micro-motor operates the bulldozer blade (retaining the blade was important to me, as it is a rather unique feature of the Tatra 813). A PF-L motor controls the lifting of the bridge cradle; one PF-M motor operates the winch for lowering the bridge, another PF-M motor handles the winch for unfolding the bridge, and a third PF-M motor—located directly inside the bridge—controls the deployment of the side extensions. The entire system is powered by two Buwizz 2.0 units. The bridge can be easily detached from the laying mechanism: simply disconnect the cables and the motor wire for the side extensions, then drive the chassis slightly forward. The bridge is strong enough to support the weight of the chassis. Together, the chassis and bridge weigh 3.75 kilograms.

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: I don't have project files but from my memory: 1. Each ring is 2 ring gears (8 pieces) connected side by side, so that the complete piece is 2 studs wide. The two halves are offset by 45 degrees so that the connection points don't line up. That improves rigidity. 2. On the bottom, the outside of the ring rests on rollers. 3. From the inside, rings are held in place by gears. 4. From the sides, rings are supported by ball pins resting in the groove/slot just below the teeth. 5. The two rings are separated by train wheels riding inside the groove/slot. Here are some photos (rear ring is partially disassembled, that's why it is 1 stud thick):
